title: Initial biodeterioration of polyethylene, polystyrene, and polyvinyl chloride microplastics  Pseudomonas monteilii  isolated from plastic wash sludge in Iraq
content: Plastic pollution poses a significant environmental threat due to the persistence and accumulation of synthetic polymers in diverse ecosystems. This study evaluated indigenous bacteria from plastic-polluted sites in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq, for their ability to degrade low-density polyethylene (LDPE), polystyrene (PS), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) microplastics. From enrichment cultures, a potential degrader was identified through biochemical profiling and 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Pseudomonas monteilii (strain HH187, 99% similarity), demonstrated enhanced growth using these plastics as the sole carbon source. Over 10 days, CFU mL−1 counts (log10) increased from 8.0 to 8.66, 8.36, and 8.20 for LDPE, PS, and PVC, respectively. Gravimetric analysis revealed modest but reproducible net mass losses of approximately 2.0–2.5% for LDPE, 1.4–1.6% for PS, and 1.1–1.3% for PVC after correction for abiotic controls. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy indicated polymer-specific surface modifications, including oxidative functionalization and alterations in C–Cl-associated vibrations in PVC, while the primary polymer backbones remained largely intact. Gas chromatography–mass spectrometry revealed polymer-dependent alterations in extractable compound profiles, including fatty acid methyl esters and plasticizer-derived phthalates, which were absent or below identification thresholds in control samples. Scanning electron microscopy demonstrated surface-associated structures and morphological changes consistent with microbial–polymer interaction. Collectively, these results identify P. monteilii HH187 as capable of surface colonization and initiating early-stage surface modifications on microplastics, representing the first documentation of this species' interaction with LDPE, PS, and PVC.
